status_summary: No transfer of the EEOC's federal-employee functions to the MSPB or of OSC investigative functions to OPM was found. The administration has instead moved several appeal categories away from the MSPB: Executive Order 14284 (signed 2025-04-24) let the OPM Director set the appeal procedures for probationary terminations, and OPM final rules published 2026-08-03 and effective 2026-09-02 give OPM, not the MSPB, appeals of probationary terminations (on limited grounds), reductions in force affecting non-SES employees, and suitability actions. The MSPB removed those categories from its jurisdiction list effective the same day, the OPM rules leave claims under EEOC-enforced laws and other independent bases in their own forums, and the EEOC proposed on 2026-08-28 to restructure its federal-sector complaint process inside the Commission, with employees choosing between an agency mixed-case complaint and an MSPB appeal but not both. A joint OPM and MSPB proposal of 2026-07-02 keeps the MSPB as reviewer of performance and misconduct removals and changes only how it reviews penalties, so it does not consolidate appeals at the MSPB.

timeline.event: Executive Order 14284 (published 2025-04-29) creates Civil Service Rule XI, under which the OPM Director may set by regulation the circumstances and procedures for appeals of probationary and trial-period terminations, and makes the subpart H probationary procedures inoperative. OPM later published a June 2025 rule rescinding subpart H.

OPM and the MSPB jointly proposed rules on performance-based and adverse actions and on MSPB review of them, keeping the MSPB as the appeal forum, replacing mandatory weighing of the Douglas factors with a totality-of-the-circumstances penalty test and limiting grievance arbitration of short suspensions; the proposal moves no EEOC or OSC function. The comment period was reopened on 2026-09-15.

OPM publishes the final rule Streamlining Probationary and Trial Period Appeals (effective 2026-09-02): appeals go to OPM, not the MSPB, limited to partisan-political or marital-status discrimination and to procedural failures where termination rests on pre-appointment reasons. Employees cannot attach EEOC-law claims, which go to the EEOC. OPM says the MSPB's former role was regulatory, not statutory.

OPM publishes the final rule Reduction in Force Appeals (effective 2026-09-02, for RIF notices issued on or after that date): OPM replaces the MSPB as adjudicator for non-SES employees furloughed more than 30 days, separated or demoted by a RIF, in a record-based process with a stated no-judicial-review provision. Pending MSPB appeals stay with the MSPB.

OPM publishes the final rule Suitability Action Appeals (effective 2026-09-02): OPM replaces the MSPB for part 731 suitability appeals by applicants, appointees and employees. The rule keeps the MSPB, EEOC, FLRA, OSC and other forums available where they have independent jurisdiction.

The MSPB publishes Appellate Jurisdiction Update II, removing probationary terminations, reductions in force and suitability actions from its jurisdiction list in 5 CFR 1201.3(a), effective 2026-09-02. It keeps hearing cases tied to actions taken before that date.

The EEOC proposes revising 29 CFR part 1614 to speed federal-sector EEO complaints inside the Commission, including ending mandatory pre-complaint counseling and the automatic hearing right, and requiring employees to pick either an agency mixed-case complaint or an MSPB appeal. Comments closed 2026-09-28. The visible text shows no transfer of functions to the MSPB or OPM.

Instead, OPM final rules published 2026-08-03 moved probationary, reduction-in-force and suitability appeals from the MSPB to OPM, and a joint OPM and MSPB proposal of 2026-07-02 keeps the MSPB as reviewer while changing penalty review. The reginfo.gov Unified Agenda (Agency Rule List - 2026) lists these OPM appeal rules (RINs 3206-AO96, AO97, AO99) and the joint accountability entries, none touching the EEOC or OSC; the EEOC list has no federal-sector transfer and OSC has no list.
